article.body:
Systems are currently being evaluated on their ability to manage resources while solving problems they define themselves. This requires a process called metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. Research suggests that for an intelligent agent to effectively allocate resources between planning and taking action, it must be able to resolve conflicting internal demands. If a system cannot separate its initial programming from the problems it generates, it risks getting stuck in cycles of error. [1]

To understand how preferences form, think of an athlete who relies on a device to plan their training. If the device suggests every movement, the athlete might stop listening to their own body signals, a phenomenon we call outsourcing. Our work explores whether autonomous systems experience similar patterns, where accumulated experience leads to stable but potentially rigid preferences. Researchers are examining how this path dependence affects a system's ability to maintain flexibility when it encounters new, unexpected environments. [1]

We are also studying how agents communicate to align their goals. In multi-agent settings, systems use structured frameworks to coordinate information exchange. By categorizing problems into distinct stages like formulation, knowledge representation, and evaluation, we can observe how agents might eventually identify their own foundational assumptions. However, identifying these deep-seated premises remains difficult, as it is unclear if an agent can reliably distinguish between genuine insights and simple data noise without external help. [1]

A key challenge is defining what makes a problem worthwhile for an agent to solve. Current approaches use discrepancy-driven evaluation, which means the system looks for gaps between what it knows and what it observes to maintain its relevance. While this helps in structured environments, we are unsure if these criteria can scale to the complex, unstructured world of scientific inquiry. If a system is left to its own devices, can it recognize when its own foundational rules are no longer working? [1]

Summary

We are studying whether AI systems can set their own goals and learn from their own experiences. We want to know if they can change their underlying rules safely or if they will always need a human to check their work. We are using concepts like 'thinking about thinking' to map how these systems make decisions. We still do not know if a machine can truly judge the importance of its own findings. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: We are investigating whether intelligent systems can independently identify meaningful problems and form stable preferences, a process that moves beyond merely following initial instructions.
article.lens: Our work examines how autonomous agents manage self-correction and goal formation by bridging insights from cognitive science, multi-agent communication, and automated problem formulation.
article.title: Navigating the Foundations of Autonomous Goal Setting

In dynamic and partially observable environments, effective communication is crucial for reducing uncertainty and enabling coordination. While research in multi-agent communication (MA-Comm) spans diverse methods and paradigms, its central challenges can often be understood through the guiding lens of the Five Ws of communication: who talks to whom, when to speak, what to convey, and why communication is beneficial. These questions provide an intuitive thread across different approaches, even when not used as explicit section divisions. Progress in this field has been rapid. Within the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework, early work emphasized static, hand-designed protocols, while later approaches introduced trainable, end-to-end communication models optimized with deep learning. This shift sparked interest in emergent language, where agents develop symbolic or structured messaging strategies through interaction. More recently, large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities, enabling natural language as a medium for reasoning, planning, and collaboration in more open-ended environments. Despite this momentum, there is still no dedicated survey that brings together these different lines of work. Most existing reviews focus narrowly on MARL, without fully addressing how communication is evolving from simple message passing to symbolic reasoning and language use. This paper aims to fill that gap. We provide a structured survey of MA-Comm, spanning traditional MARL approaches and emergent language studies. In light of growing interest in agentic and embodied AI, we also examine how LLMs are reshaping communication in both MARL contexts and broader multi-agent ecosystems. By using the Five Ws as a conceptual lens, our goal is to clarify the landscape, highlight key trends, and provide a foundation for future research at the intersection of communication, coordination, and learning in multi-agent systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175760290.08279849/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 9, 11]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7648642\", \"title\": [\"HealthGuard-MARL: Emergent Sleeper-Cell Fraud in a Multi-Agent Healthcare Insurance Market A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Healthcare Fraud Detection\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Healthcare fraud costs the United States an estimated $300 billion annually [1]. Current detection systems are retrospective and static, failing against adaptive, patient adversaries. We present HealthGuard-MARL, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework in which a saboteur hospital agent discovers a sleeper-cell fraud strategy: behave honestly to accumulate trust, strike with inflated claims at peak trust, absorb the penalty, and repeat, entirely through reward maximisation, with no scripted fraud instructions. We replicate the Kerr &amp; Cohen (2006, 2009) Value Imbalance attack in a healthcare trust-audit simulation and make four original contributions: (1) a 30-seed significance test demonstrating the strategy is statistically robust (paired t(29) = 9.36, p &lt; 10-6 , Cohen's d = 1.71, 100% directional consistency); (2) a three-metric behavioural distinctness test showing the learned policy is qualitatively different from a maximum-intensity hand-coded threshold rule (all p &lt; 0.0001, Bonferroni-corrected); (3) a learning insurer that decisively defeats the sleeper (19/20 vs. 1/20 runs, non-overlapping CIs); and (4) a monitoring-cost phase transition that governs who wins the arms race. ABSTRACT
Communication is an effective mechanism for coordinating the behaviors of multiple agents, broad-
ening their views of the environment, and to support their collaborations. In the field of multi-agent
deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), agents can improve the overall learning performance and
achieve their objectives by communication. Agents can communicate various types of messages,
either to all agents or to specific agent groups, or conditioned on specific constraints. With the grow-
ing body of research work in MADRL with communication (Comm-MADRL), there is a lack of a
systematic and structural approach to distinguish and classify existing Comm-MADRL approaches.
In this paper, we survey recent works in the Comm-MADRL field and consider various aspects of
communication that can play a role in designing and developing multi-agent reinforcement learn-
ing systems. With these aspects in mind, we propose 9 dimensions along which Comm-MADRL
approaches can be analyzed, developed, and compared. By projecting existing works into the multi-
dimensional space, we discover interesting trends. We also propose some novel directions for de-
signing future Comm-MADRL systems through exploring possible combinations of the dimensions.

1 Introduction
Many real-world scenarios, such as autonomous driving [1], sensor networks [2], robotics [3] and game-playing [4, 5],
can be modeled as multi-agent systems. Such multi-agent systems can be designed and developed using multi-agent
reinforcement learning (MARL) techniques to learn the behavior of individual agents, which can be cooperative,
competitive, or a mixture of them. As agents are often distributed in the environment where they only have access to
their local observations rather than the complete state of the environment, partial observability becomes an essential
assumption in MARL [6, 7, 8]. Moreover, MARL suffers from the non-stationary issue [9], since each agent faces a
dynamic environment that can be influenced by the changing and adapting policies of other agents. Communication
has been viewed as a vital means to tackle the problems of partial observability and non-stationary in MARL. Agents
can communicate individual information, e.g., observations, intentions, experiences, or derived features, to have a
broader view of the environment, which in turn allows them to make well-informed decisions [9, 10].
Due to the recent success of deep learning [11] and its application to reinforcement learning [12], multi-agent deep
reinforcement learning (MADRL) has witnessed great achievements in recent years, where agents can process high-
dimensional data and have generalization ability in large state and action spaces [7, 8]. We notice that a large number
